title: Holy Land, Honest Scales, and the Prince's Offerings
summary: A holy district is set apart in the land for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, and the city, with land on either side for the prince. God commands Israel's princes to stop their violence and seizing of land, and requires honest weights and measures. The people's offerings go to the prince, who must provide the sacrifices for the feasts, and the calendar opens with rites to purify the sanctuary, Passover, and the feast of the seventh month.
story: Chapter 44 ordered the people who serve in the temple; chapter 45 orders the land around it and the ruler who governs it. The vision looks back on the last kings of Judah, who used their power to enrich themselves and dispossess the poor, and builds safeguards into the land itself. Giving the prince a fixed estate means he has no excuse to take anyone else's. The chapter briefly anticipates the full division of the land in chapters 47 and 48, and it links justice in the marketplace with worship at the altar: honest scales come just before the offerings, because God will not accept sacrifices bought with fraud.
historical:
Ezekiel had watched Judah's kings abuse their power. Jehoiakim built a palace with forced labor (Jeremiah 22:13-17), and the prophets repeatedly accused the ruling class of seizing fields and houses (Micah 2:2; Isaiah 5:8). The story of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) shows how a king could take a family's inheritance by legal fraud. Ezekiel 34 condemned Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves instead of the flock. Verses 8 and 9 answer that history directly: "Cease your violence and oppression, and do what is just and right."

The ruler in Ezekiel's vision is called the prince (nasi) rather than king. Earlier in the book, God promised that "My servant David" would be prince among his people (34:24; 37:25). The prince of chapters 44 to 46 has a special place in worship and is responsible for supplying the public offerings, but he is not a priest, he offers a sin offering for himself (verse 22), and he has sons who inherit (46:16). Most interpreters therefore see him as an idealized ruler of a restored Israel rather than a direct portrait of the Messiah, though the book's hopes for a Davidic prince stand behind him.
cultural:
Weights and measures were a constant temptation in ancient trade. Merchants weighed silver on balance scales against stones, and a heavier stone for buying and a lighter one for selling was an easy way to cheat. The law and the prophets condemn it again and again (Leviticus 19:35-36; Amos 8:5; Proverbs 11:1). Ezekiel sets fixed standards: the ephah for dry goods and the bath for liquids are both a tenth of a homer, and the mina is sixty shekels (twenty plus twenty-five plus fifteen, perhaps reflecting the sizes of actual weight stones). The contributions are modest and proportional: a sixtieth of grain, a hundredth of oil, and one sheep in two hundred.

The calendar differs in notable ways from the one in the Law of Moses. It opens with purification of the sanctuary on the first and seventh days of the first month, rites that have no exact parallel in the Pentateuch. It keeps Passover and the seven-day feast in the seventh month (Tabernacles, though not named), but it does not mention the Feast of Weeks or the Day of Atonement, and the numbers of animals differ from Numbers 28 and 29. These differences troubled later Jewish teachers; a tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud says that a rabbi named Hananiah son of Hezekiah labored long to reconcile Ezekiel's rules with the Torah so that the book would not be set aside.
literary: The chapter is legal prose within the vision, made up of three blocks. The first (verses 1 to 8) is a land survey, precise and symmetrical, with the sanctuary at the center of concentric zones of holiness. The second (verses 9 to 17) is prophetic exhortation followed by regulation, and it begins with the kind of direct address typical of the earlier oracles: "Enough, O princes of Israel" (verse 9). The third (verses 18 to 25) is a festival calendar. The chapter moves from space to economy to time, bringing each under God's order. Measurements are in cubits, and elsewhere in the vision the long cubit of about 20 inches (52 centimeters) is used, which makes the holy district roughly eight miles (13 kilometers) long. Together with the city's portion it forms a square of 25,000 cubits (48:20).

outline.t: The holy district for the sanctuary, priests, and Levites
The city's portion and the prince's land
Justice for princes and honest weights and measures
The people's offerings and the prince's duty
Purifying the sanctuary in the first month
Passover and the feast of the seventh month

doctrines.note: The sanctuary sits at the center of the land, surrounded by zones for priests, Levites, and city. Holiness shapes geography: the whole land is ordered around God's presence.
Honest scales and fair land tenure are placed right beside worship. God's law treats economic justice as part of covenant faithfulness, not a separate matter.

The offerings are given "to make atonement for the people" (verse 15), and even the sanctuary needs purifying for those who sin unintentionally or in ignorance (verse 20). God provides a way for a people who still fail to live near him.

words.note: Nasi, prince, leader, or chief, literally one who is lifted up. Ezekiel prefers it to king (melek) for Israel's future ruler, perhaps to mark a humbler, more accountable office after the failures of the monarchy.

Terumah, contribution or portion, something lifted off and set apart for God. It names both the holy district of land (verse 1) and the people's offerings (verse 13). Land and produce alike are first given to God.
Tsedeq, righteousness or rightness. The honest scales of verse 10 are literally scales of righteousness. The word links everyday commerce with the character of God, who is righteous.

Kipper, to make atonement, to cover or to purge. In verses 15, 17, and 20 it describes offerings that remove the barrier sin creates between a holy God and his people and that cleanse the sanctuary itself.

christ: The chapter's ideal ruler protects his people instead of taking from them, and its worship centers on sacrifices that make atonement. The New Testament brings both together in Jesus. He is the Davidic ruler who came "not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45), the opposite of the princes who oppressed God's people. He is also the sacrifice to which the offerings pointed: "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7), and by his one offering the church has been sanctified "once for all" (Hebrews 10:10). Unlike Ezekiel's prince, Jesus needed no sin offering for himself. Hebrews calls the law's sacrifices "a shadow of the good things to come" (Hebrews 10:1), and Christians read Ezekiel's offerings in that light.

hard.q: Why does Ezekiel's worship calendar differ from the Law of Moses?
hard.a: The differences are real: new purification rites in the first month, a different number of sacrificial animals, and no mention of the Feast of Weeks or the Day of Atonement. Interpreters explain them in several ways. Some see Ezekiel as giving a new, idealized law for the restored community, not meant to repeal Moses but to express the holiness of the new age in fresh terms. Others think Ezekiel records priestly practice of his own time, which varied from the written Torah. Those who expect a literal future temple often argue that the changes suit a different era of God's dealings with Israel, including memorial rather than atoning sacrifices, though the text itself uses the word atonement. Many Christian interpreters read the vision as symbolic, so that the changed details signal that the old order is not being simply restored. Jewish tradition felt the difficulty keenly and resolved it by harmonizing the texts. The shared point is that worship in the restored community would be ordered, generous, and centered on God's holiness.

questions: Ezekiel places honest scales right beside the offerings. Where does your faith touch the way you buy, sell, pay, or charge?
The prince was given land so that he would not take land from others. What safeguards could protect you from using your power at others' expense?
The purification rites were for those who sin unintentionally or in ignorance. How does it change your view of God to know he provides for failures you do not even notice?
